msgs.pub:
Much of the damage I have done to my accounts came on days I felt I had to act.

The Hippocratic writings tell doctors to help, or at least to do no harm.

Those doctors knew the urge to treat was itself a risk. A worried patient wants a pill. A worried trader wants an order.

The market drops, and the hands go to the keyboard.

Sometimes the right treatment is nothing.

I can be wrong here. Some drops do need a cut, and my stop handles those.

The rest of the time, I watch and leave the account alone.

A trade you skip in panic never needs repairing.

msgs.title: The hardest trade to make is leaving after you won.
msgs.pub:
The hardest trade to make is leaving after you won.

Rome once called Cincinnatus from his small farm to save the city in a crisis.

Livy says he won, gave the power back after sixteen days, and went home to plough.

Most traders do the opposite. One big win and they stay in the chair, hunting for the next one.

The win becomes the reason to keep risking it.

I have no rule for the exact top. Nobody has one.

When a trade pays what I planned, I close it and go back to my field.

Power you hold too long starts holding you.

msgs.title: Nobody can tell you the day a rally turned into a bubble.
msgs.pub:
Nobody can tell you the day a rally turned into a bubble.

The Greek logician Eubulides had a puzzle for this. One grain of sand is no heap. Add one grain, still no heap.

Keep adding, and at some point you have a heap. Nobody can name the grain.

Markets work the same way.

Each day up looks reasonable next to the day before, so the perma-bulls never find the grain that changed it.

I can't name the grain either.

So I stop asking for the exact day. I trim when the pile looks big from far away.

Step back far enough and the heap is obvious.

Around 𝟱𝟮𝟰, Boethius sat in a cell waiting to be executed. He had been rich and powerful.

They took the ride up as proof of skill, and they will take the ride down as an injustice.

Maybe this wheel keeps rising a while longer. I have no idea how long.

I keep my size where a full turn down will not break me.

The wheel never promised to stop at the top.

Busy accounts make brokers rich.

The orders that pay are the rare ones.

A few good businesses, bought when nobody wanted them, then left alone for years.

Picture someone who places one order every three or four years.

Next to the active trader glued to the screen, they look lazy.

Give it a decade and the lazy one usually has more.

Doing nothing is a position too, and it is the hardest one to hold.

msgs.title: Some traders cannot take good news at face value.
msgs.pub:
Some traders cannot take good news at face value.

The market rallies, so they decide the smart money already sold to retail.

Then real good news lands, and they call it bait to unload stock.

Then the dip gets bought, and they call that a bull trap too.

Every fact gets flipped one more time.

From the inside it feels like deep thinking.

I have been that trader. The rally kept going while I kept flipping.

Sometimes good news is just good news.
